interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the two healthy lines' charging currents swinging to 60° apart and adding head to tail to three times one line's healthy current when you switch the fault onto L1.
interactive.title: The cable that is a capacitor
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Twelve small screens on one picture, with Back and Continue. Five show an idea and seven ask you to try it. No marks and no timers.

The picture. A switchboard on the left feeds a load on the right through a three-line feeder. L1 is on top, then L2, then L3. A thick bar under the feeder is the hull, which is earth. All along the run, small capacitors join each line to the hull, in three rows. Each one stands for a stretch of cable, because the copper and the hull are two plates with the insulation between them. A small drive card sits by the load. It has its own capacitors to the hull, drawn only when its switch is on. Beside the feeder is a phasor panel. It draws each line's current into the hull as an arrow, in milliamps, to one scale.

The controls sit under the picture, in a row that wraps on a phone. A mode picker has three buttons: Healthy, Fault on L1 and Person on L1. A slider, Cable length, runs from 0.5 to 16 km in steps of 0.5 km. Then come a switch, Ten drives' filters, and a button, 480 V check. In Fault on L1 a solid link joins L1 to the hull. In Person on L1 a figure stands on the hull with one hand on L1, and there is no fault.

The readouts sit in tiles that wrap onto more rows on a phone. They show from screen 3 on. While the arrows swing, Current to earth follows them. Capacitance a line is in µF. Charging current a line, healthy, is in mA. Current to earth is in mA, and it shows the fault current or the body current. Below them, a small plot of Current to earth against cable length, with a dot at the present setting.

The rule it computes. Take a 440 V, 60 Hz supply. When healthy, each line sits 440 ÷ 1.732 = 254 V from earth. Say each line has 0.25 µF to the hull for every kilometre of cable, and each drive's filter adds 0.1 µF a line. So C, the capacitance a line, is 0.25 × length. Switching in the ten drives adds 1 µF. A capacitor on AC passes ω × C × V. Here ω = 2π × 60 = 377, and V is the voltage across it. Healthy, each line passes ω × C × 254 V. That is its charging current. The three arrows sit 120° apart, so they close into a triangle and add to zero. With the fault on L1, the hull moves to L1, as in the shifting triangle. L1's capacitors have 0 V across them and its arrow shrinks to nothing. L2's and L3's capacitors hold 440 V, so each arrow grows 1.73 times. The two arrows swing to 60° apart and slide head to tail. A third arrow, from tail to head, shows their sum. That sum is the fault current: 3 × ω × C × 254 V. In Person on L1, the body is an example 1,000 Ω. All the capacitance together acts in series with it: Current to earth = 254 V ÷ the size of (1,000 Ω in series with the reactance of 3 × C). In Fault on L1 the plot is a straight line, through zero with the drives off. In Person on L1 it is a curve that levels off. The 480 V check sets a 480 V supply, 277 V a line. It gives 3.3 µF a line, a reactance of 800 Ω.

The opening setting is 4 km with no drives. There C = 1 µF, and each line passes 96 mA healthy. With the fault on, L2 and L3 pass 166 mA each and the fault current is 287 mA. The body current is 190 mA. At 8 km, or 4 km with the drives: C = 2 µF, 192 mA healthy, fault current 575 mA. At 0.5 km: body current 36 mA. At 16 km with the drives: C = 5 µF, 479 mA healthy, fault current 1.44 A.

Screen 1, show. Healthy, 4 km, drives off, the phasor panel and readouts hidden. The words: "Every conductor near the hull is a capacitor. The copper is one plate and the hull is the other, with the insulation between. So a feeder has small capacitors from each line to the hull all along its run. Windings and drive filters add more. An insulated supply has no tie to earth. Yet it is joined to the hull through all this capacitance.[^1]" Still: Healthy, 4 km.

Screen 2, try it. "Each line has 1 µF to the hull. What is that capacitance's reactance at 60 Hz?" Three choices, in this order: "About 377 Ω"; "About 2,650 Ω"; "Infinite, as a capacitor blocks current". Right, the second. Hint for the second: "377 is ω, 2π × 60. The reactance is 1 divided by ω × C." Hint for the third: "That holds for steady DC. On AC the plates charge and discharge every half cycle, so current flows in the wires either side." Why: "A capacitor's reactance is 1 ÷ (2π × f × C). Here that is 1 ÷ (2π × 60 × 0.000001) = 2,650 Ω. With 254 V across it, about 96 mA flows." A right Check labels one row of capacitors 2,650 Ω. Read: "Each line has 1 µF to the hull. What is that capacitance's reactance at 60 Hz?"

Screen 3, show. Healthy, 4 km, the phasor panel shown. The words: "Each line charges its capacitors one way, then the other, 60 times a second. That flow in the line is its charging current. With 1 µF a line on 440 V, each line passes 96 mA. The panel draws the three as arrows, 120° apart like their voltages. Laid head to tail, they close into a triangle. So they cancel in the hull. Each line's current comes back through the other two lines' capacitance. There is no tie to the star point." Still: Healthy, 4 km.

Screen 4, try it. "With no fault, each line pushes 96 mA into the hull. What do the three add up to?" Three choices, in this order: "287 mA, three times 96 mA"; "96 mA, the same as one line"; "Zero, in this balanced picture". Right, the third. Hint for the second: "They are 120° apart, so they do not add as plain numbers. Lay them head to tail." Hint for the third: "Lay all three arrows head to tail. Where does the last one end?" Why: "Three equal arrows 120° apart close into a triangle, so they add to zero. It works like a balanced load's neutral. A real system is a little unbalanced, so a little is left over." A right Check slides the three arrows head to tail. Read: "With no fault, each line pushes 96 mA into the hull. What do the three add up to?"

Screen 5, show. Fault on L1, 4 km. The words: "Now L1 faults solidly to the hull. The hull moves to L1, so L1's capacitors have no voltage across them and pass nothing. L2's and L3's capacitors now hold 440 V instead of 254 V. So each passes 1.73 times as much, 166 mA. Both are measured from L1's corner of the triangle, so they sit 60° apart. Head to tail they add to 287 mA, three times one line's healthy current." Read: "With a solid fault on L1, L1's capacitors pass nothing. L2 and L3 each pass 166 mA, 60° apart. Head to tail they add to 287 mA." Still: Fault on L1, 4 km.

Screen 6, try it. "With L1 faulted solidly, what carries the fault current back round to the supply?" Three choices, in this order: "The capacitance of L2 and L3 to the hull"; "Nothing carries it, as a capacitor blocks current"; "A tie from the hull to the star point". Right, the first. Hint for the second: "On AC a capacitor passes current as its plates charge and discharge. 440 V across 1 µF at 60 Hz passes 166 mA." Hint for the third: "There is no tie. That is what makes the supply insulated." Why: "The current leaves the supply on L2 and L3 and crosses their capacitance into the hull. It runs along the hull to the fault and back through it into L1.[^2] The windings close the loop." A right Check lights the loop. Read: "With L1 faulted solidly, what carries the fault current back round to the supply?"

Screen 7, show. Fault on L1, the slider moving from 4 km to 8 km. The words: "Two arrows 60° apart add to 1.73 times one of them. The same geometry makes 440 V 1.73 times 254 V. Each arrow was 1.73 times the healthy current, so the sum is 3 times it. The rule is fault current = 3 × ω × C × V_phase. Capacitance grows with the system. Every metre of cable and every filter adds some in parallel. Watch the cable go from 4 km to 8 km. C doubles to 2 µF and the fault current doubles to 575 mA." Read: "At 8 km of cable, C is 2 µF a line and the fault current is 575 mA, twice the 4 km figure. The plot is a straight line through zero." Still: Fault on L1, 8 km.

Screen 8, try it. "A 440 V system has 1 µF a line, and a first fault passes 287 mA. Ten drives are added, each with 0.1 µF a line in its filter. What does a first fault pass now?" Three choices, in this order: "287 mA, as the cable is the same"; "About 1.15 A, four times as much"; "About 575 mA". Right, the third. Hint for the first: "The filters are capacitors to the hull too, in parallel with the cable. Ten of them add 1 µF a line." Hint for the second: "C has doubled. The current goes up in step with C, not with its square." Why: "Capacitors in parallel add, so ten filters add 1 µF a line. C doubles to 2 µF, so the fault current doubles to about 575 mA. The larger the system, the lower its impedance to earth.[^3]" A right Check switches the drives' filters in. Read: "A 440 V system has 1 µF a line, and a first fault passes 287 mA. Ten drives are added, each with 0.1 µF a line in its filter. What does a first fault pass now?"

Screen 9, show. Person on L1, 4 km. The words: "Take the fault away. A person stands on the hull and touches L1. Say the body is 1,000 Ω. The person becomes the fault, and the cables' capacitance closes the loop. With 1 µF a line, about 190 mA flows through the body. The body's resistance holds it below a solid fault's 287 mA. That is still over six times the 30 mA a socket RCD is rated to trip at. Even with 0.5 km of cable it is about 36 mA. An insulated supply is not safe to touch." Read: "A person on the hull touches L1 of a healthy system with 1 µF a line. About 190 mA flows through the body, back through the cables' capacitance." Still: Person on L1, 4 km.

Screen 10, try it, the first of three mixed puzzles. "You stand on the hull and touch L1, first on a small insulated system, then on a big one. Both are 440 V and healthy. Which passes more current through you?" Three choices, in this order: "The same on both, as the voltage is the same"; "The big one, as its capacitance to the hull is larger"; "Neither passes any, as there is no other end of the circuit". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "The current comes back through the cables' capacitance. More capacitance means less reactance in the loop." Hint for the third: "The other end is there. Every cable is a capacitor to the hull you stand on." Why: "The cables' capacitance closes the loop through you, as it would for a fault. A big system has more of it, so less reactance in the loop. With 0.5 km of cable about 36 mA flows. With 4 km it is about 190 mA." A right Check switches to Person on L1, at 4 km. Read: "You stand on the hull and touch L1, first on a small insulated system, then on a big one. Both are 440 V and healthy. Which passes more current through you?"

Screen 11, try it. "A 440 V, 60 Hz insulated system has 5 µF a line. Healthy, each line passes 479 mA. What does a solid first fault pass?" Three choices, in this order: "About 1.44 A"; "About 830 mA"; "479 mA, the same as one line". Right, the first. Hint for the second: "That is one healthy line at 440 V. Two of them add, 60° apart." Hint for the third: "The fault lifts L2 and L3 to 440 V, so their currents grow. Then two of them add." Why: "The fault current is three times one line's healthy charging current. 3 × 479 mA = 1.44 A. A big system's first fault passes amps, not milliamps." A right Check sets 16 km with the drives on and the fault on L1. Read: "A 440 V, 60 Hz insulated system has 5 µF a line. Healthy, each line passes 479 mA. What does a solid first fault pass?"

Screen 12, try it. "A 480 V, 60 Hz insulated system has 277 V a phase. Each line's capacitance to the hull has a reactance of 800 Ω. What does a solid first fault pass?" Three choices, in this order: "About 0.35 A"; "About 1.04 A"; "About 0.60 A". Right, the second. Hint for the first: "That is one line's healthy current, 277 ÷ 800. The fault passes three times as much." Hint for the third: "That is one healthy line at 480 V. Two of them add, 60° apart." Why: "One line's healthy current is 277 ÷ 800 = 0.35 A. Three times that is 1.04 A.[^2]" A right Check presses 480 V check, with the fault on L1. The caption under the picture then gives the 480 V values. Read: "A 480 V, 60 Hz insulated system has 277 V a phase. Each line's capacitance to the hull has a reactance of 800 Ω. What does a solid first fault pass?"

Every figure on these screens is an example value or worked from the rule above.
interactive.ignores: The picture lumps each line's capacitance into a few capacitors. Really it is spread along every metre of cable and every winding. It gives all three lines the same capacitance and draws the fault as a solid join. It leaves out insulation resistance, which lets a little more current through. The 0.25 µF a kilometre and 0.1 µF a drive are example values, and real cables and filters vary widely. A body is not a fixed 1,000 Ω. The currents are r.m.s. values of alternating currents, so the arrows really turn sixty times a second.

explain.text:
An insulated supply has no tie to earth, but it is still joined to it. Every cable and winding is a capacitor to the hull. So the whole system is joined to earth through its capacitance.[^1] A solid first earth fault drives current round through that capacitance. It is three times what one line passes when healthy. The bigger the system, the bigger that current.

Take one line of a feeder. Its copper and the hull are two plates, with the insulation between them. On a 60 Hz supply the plates charge one way, then the other, 60 times a second. So a current flows in the line, even though no charge crosses the insulation. That is the line's [[charging current]]. A capacitor passes ω × C × V. Here ω = 2π × 60 = 377, C is the capacitance and V the voltage across it. Say each line has 1 µF to the hull on a 440 V supply. Healthy, each line sits 254 V from earth, so it passes 377 × 0.000001 × 254 = 96 mA. The three currents sit 120° apart, like their voltages. Laid head to tail they close into a triangle. So they cancel in the hull, as a balanced load's neutral current does.

Now L1 faults solidly to the hull. The hull moves to L1, as in the shifting triangle. L1's capacitance now has no voltage across it and passes nothing. L2 and L3 each sit 440 V from the hull, 1.73 times their healthy voltage. So each passes 1.73 × 96 = 166 mA. Both voltages are measured from L1's corner of the triangle, so they sit 60° apart. So do their currents. Two equal arrows 60° apart add to 1.73 times one of them. So the sum is 1.73 × 1.73 = 3 times the healthy current, about 287 mA. There is no tie for it to go home by. It leaves the supply on L2 and L3 and crosses their capacitance into the hull. Then it returns through the fault into L1.[^2]

C grows with the system. Every length of cable and every drive's filter adds capacitance in parallel, so the values add. The larger the system, the lower its impedance to earth.[^3] Double the capacitance and the fault current doubles. A small system passes milliamps. A 480 V system with 800 Ω of reactance a line passes 1.04 A.[^2] The same capacitance closes the loop through a person who touches one line. So an insulated supply is not safe to touch. This is a simplified model. It gives every line the same capacitance. It also ignores insulation resistance, which adds a little more current. A fault through some resistance passes less. **A solid first earth fault on an insulated supply passes three times one line's healthy charging current: 3 × ω × C × V_phase. So it grows with the system.**

analogy.text: Put enough computers on one 30 mA RCD and it can trip with no fault anywhere. Each one's mains filter has small capacitors to earth, and their leakage currents add. An insulated system's cables, windings and drive filters add up the same way. So a big system has a lot of capacitance to the hull.
analogy.breaks: On that RCD circuit the leakage returns to an earthed star point all the time. On an insulated supply the three healthy currents largely cancel. Their sum, up to three times one line's, only appears when a fault or a person gives it a way through.

practice.text:
- Safety first: an insulated supply can drive a dangerous current through you with no fault on it at all. The cables' capacitance closes the loop. Isolate and prove dead as on any job.
- To estimate a first fault's current, find the phase voltage: the line voltage ÷ 1.732.
- Add up the capacitance a line to earth: cables, windings and drive filters, all in parallel.
- Work out one line's healthy charging current: 2π × the frequency × C × V_phase.
- Multiply by 3 for a solid first fault's current. A fault through some resistance passes less.
- Expect it to grow as feeders and drives are added.

**Rules of thumb:** On 440 V at 60 Hz, each microfarad a line adds about 0.29 A to the first-fault current. About 10 µF on a 277 V phase carries about 1 A of charging current.[^4]

**Worked example:** A 440 V, 60 Hz insulated system has 4 km of cable at 0.25 µF a kilometre a line. That is 1 µF a line. Ten drives add 0.1 µF a line each, another 1 µF. So C is 2 µF a line. One line's healthy charging current is 377 × 0.000002 × 254 = 192 mA. A solid first fault passes three times that, about 575 mA.

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking no current can flow with no return path. The capacitance is the return path.
- Treating a capacitor as a barrier. It blocks steady DC but passes AC.
- Assuming a first fault always passes only milliamps. It grows with the system, to amps on a big one.
- Multiplying by 1.73 instead of 3. That is one healthy line at line voltage. Two of them add.

sources.quote: although called ungrounded, this type of system is in reality coupled to ground through the distributed capacitance of its phase windings and conductors.

sources.title: Characteristics of different power systems neutral grounding techniques: Fact and fiction
sources.quote: there is no direct ground path back to the neutral point of the source in Figure 3b , the current must return through the distributed capacitance (insulation system) of the two unfaulted phases. As indicated, only 1.04 A will flow.

sources.title: Technical aspects IT systems
sources.quote: The limits of an IT system are largely determined by its expansion. The larger the system, the smaller the impedance between active conductors and earth.

sources.title: Transient overvoltages on ungrounded systems from intermittent ground faults
sources.quote: A capacitance of approximately 10µF on a 277 V system, then, will result in approximately 1 ampere of continuous (charging) current through that capacitance.
